questions.question: Using the brick factory and the shared river, explain the two market failures behind environmental deterioration and why each leads to overuse.
questions.expected_answer: Externalities: the factory's smoke and wash-water impose costs on the village that appear on no invoice, so the polluter's costs — and the product's price — understate the true cost; the too-cheap product is oversupplied, meaning the market produces more pollution than the full cost would justify. The commons: the river belongs to nobody, so each fisherman gains the whole benefit of one more fish while the depletion cost is shared by all; every individually sensible user takes more, and the stock collapses — the tragedy of the commons. In both cases the market obeys prices that lie, and future generations, who place no orders today, are not represented at all.

questions.question: Name the four families of environmental protection tools with a South African example of each, and state which failure each repairs plus one weakness.
questions.expected_answer: Command and control (emission standards, fishing quotas, environmental impact assessments) — sets direct legal limits; certain, but only as strong as enforcement. Market-based instruments (carbon tax, plastic bag and tyre levies, renewable subsidies, tradable permits) — price the externality so polluting stops being free; efficient, but regressive unless revenue is recycled to poor households. Property rights and community management (community fishing quotas, conservancies keeping tourism revenue) — create owners for the commons so future value is protected; allocation must be fair. International agreements (Paris Agreement) — stop free-riding since carbon ignores borders; broad but weakly enforced. No tool repairs everything, so real policy stacks them.

questions.question: Quote the Brundtland definition of sustainable development, explain the interest-versus-capital idea for renewables and non-renewables, and apply the three-legged tripod to South Africa's just transition.
questions.expected_answer: Sustainable development 'meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. Renewables (fish, forests, water) are capital that yields interest — harvest slower than regeneration and they last forever; harvest faster and they collapse. Non-renewables (coal, gold, platinum) never regenerate, so sustainability means converting their once-off proceeds into lasting assets like skills and infrastructure. Tripod applied: environmental — decarbonise coal-heavy electricity that also invites carbon border taxes; economic — build renewables fast enough to power growth; social — retrain coal workers and rebuild regions like Mpumalanga, with Just Energy Transition finance helping pay. Drop any leg — cook the climate, kill the power supply, or abandon the coal towns — and the transition fails.
